sweep_summary: Old Saxon is in the catalog as fixed-unreviewed on Holthausen 1921 (initial stress in simplex words and nominal compounds). The two title-works with stress in the title are both studies of the vowel system of weakly stressed (suffixal) syllables in the Heliand — King 1965 (Word 21, DOI 10.1080/00437956.1965.11435416, bronze OA at T&F but every download by automated download could not be reached by automated download) and Marino 1973 (Indogermanische Forschungen 78:163-168, paywalled at De Gruyter; Semantic Scholar abstract obtained and saved). Neither, from the abstract/title, addresses where main stress falls; both presuppose the handbook stressed/unstressed distinction, so they are silent on the catalog's classification (low priority). The best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Gallée 1910 §21 (already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass), which independently confirms first-syllable stress in nouns, simplex and compound, native and borrowed, with prefix details matching Holthausen; it does not supersede Holthausen 1921.

new_statements.quote: § 21. Der hauptton liegt beim nomen, beim altsächsischen wie beim fremdworte, beim einfachen wie beim kompositum, auf der ersten silbe. So: sámad, técan, níðer, hímiles, físcari, wíðarmôd, wírôc, wáldand, frómod etc. — Péter, Ádam, Évan, Dávides, María etc. Nur Erodes hat die betonung Eródes 2705, 5281 und Eródes 71, 728, 548, 716 etc. ... § 22. Mit praefixen zusammengesetzte nomina haben den akzent meist auf dem praefix: ábunst, fórabodo, mísdâd, wíðersako ... Mit und ohne akzent finden sich die praefixe bi- und un- ... Das nominalpraefix gi- ist immer tonlos.
new_statements.translation: §21. In the noun — native word and loanword alike, simplex and compound alike — the main stress lies on the first syllable. Thus: sámad, técan, níðer, hímiles, físcari, wíðarmôd, wírôc, wáldand, frómod etc. — Péter, Ádam, Évan, Dávides, María etc. Only Erodes has the stress Eródes ... §22. Nouns compounded with prefixes mostly have the accent on the prefix: ábunst, fórabodo, mísdâd, wíðersako ... The prefixes bi- and un- occur both with and without accent ... The nominal prefix gi- is always unstressed.
new_statements.citation: Gallée, Johan Hendrik. 1910. Altsächsische Grammatik. 2. völlig umgearbeitete Auflage (eingeleitet von Johannes Lochner). Halle: Max Niemeyer. archive.org item altschsischegram00gall.
new_statements.reading: Fixed initial (root) stress in simplex words and nominal compounds, including loanwords; prefixed nouns usually stress the prefix, bi-/un- vary, gi- is never stressed (verbs stress the root, §24). This is the same rule as the catalog's Holthausen 1921 §§67-68 and confirms the 'fixed' coding. The file was downloaded by our earlier reading on 2026-09-16 and re-read now; the two works with stress in the title (King 1965, Marino 1973) could not be read and are studies of unstressed-syllable vowel phonology, not of stress placement.

tone.quote: 66. Nach der Stärke des Nachdrucks, mit der die einzelnen Silben eines Wortes gesprochen werden, unterscheidet man im As. wie in den andern germanischen Sprachen eine dreifache Betonung: Hauptton ('), Nebenton C) und Unbetontheit. Zur Bestim- mung derselben sind sowohl die verwandten Dialekte wie auch die Entwickelung des As. selbst heranzuziehen ; wichtige Aufschlüsse gibt auch die Metrik der poetischen Denkmäler. [...] 67. Der Hauptton liegt im einfachen Worte und bei den No- minalkompositis auf der ersten Silbe
tone.translation: §66. According to the strength of the force (Nachdruck) with which the individual syllables of a word are spoken, one distinguishes in Old Saxon, as in the other Germanic languages, a threefold accentuation: main stress ('), secondary stress (`) and unstressedness. To determine it, both the related dialects and the development of Old Saxon itself must be drawn upon; the metre of the poetic monuments also gives important information. [...] §67. The main stress lies, in the simple word and in nominal compounds, on the first syllable. (scanned text layer: 'Nebenton C)' renders the printed grave-accent sign in parentheses.)
tone.says: The grammar describes Old Saxon word prosody purely as a dynamic (stress) accent: §66 distinguishes three degrees of 'Betonung' by 'Stärke des Nachdrucks' (force of articulation) - Hauptton, Nebenton, Unbetontheit - determined from related dialects, later development and the metre of the poems; §§67-72 give initial (root) main stress, §73 secondary stress, §74 sentence accent. No pitch, musical accent or tone is mentioned anywhere in the Lautlehre; 'Ton' in Hauptton/Nebenton means stress degree…

sources.quote: The system of the weakly stressed vowels in Old Saxon represents a problem in phonological structures that underlie a non-unique assignment of graphs in an ancient language. The weakly stressed vowels in Germanic languages in general are in the process of weakening or centralizing. ... If the same process is already well along in the speech of the scribes for the Heliand, then the undefined weakening will be in competition with the conservatism of the graphic systems. The graphic alternations for weakly stressed Old Saxon vowels have been largely unexplained by traditional handbooks and variously treated by three scholars in terms of post-Bloomfieldian linguistics.
sources.note: Per the abstract, the paper is about the phonemic/graphemic system of the vowels in weakly stressed (non-initial, suffixal) syllables of the Heliand, arguing against Twaddell's four-phoneme analysis; it presupposes the stressed/weakly-stressed syllable distinction of the handbooks and does not (per the abstract) treat where the main stress falls. Full text is paywalled at De Gruyter (Unpaywall: closed; degruyterbrill.com returned a bot challenge, HTTP 202/405).
